activities.caption: the shorthand — pair each symbol with its meaning
activities.name: pbSymMatch

config.prompt: Match each symbol to what it asserts:

pairs.right: the event that A doesn't happen
A happens, or B, or both
the chance of A once you know B happened — where most real reasoning lives

config.why: The vertical bar is the whole subject in one symbol: it reshapes the sample space before any rule is applied.

activities.caption: one line of the bag-drawing method is wrong — click it
activities.name: pbBagSpot

config.prompt: One line of this bag method is wrong — click it:
lines: With replacement: P(red then red) = 4/10 × 4/10 = 0.16 — the two draws are identical situations.
Without replacement: P(red then red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15 — fewer reds (3) in a smaller bag (9).
P(exactly one red in two draws) = 4/10 × 6/9 = 24/90 — one path, one product.
Adjust the second factor for whatever the first draw removed — that single idea generates every without-replacement answer.
config.correction: Both orderings must be counted: P(red then blue) + P(blue then red) = 24/90 + 24/90 = 48/90 = 8/15.
config.why: Exactly one red can arrive in two costumes — forgetting the second path is the classic slip in two-stage products.

activities.caption: call the conditional before the recount does
activities.name: pbCondEst

config.prompt: Two dice. You are told the first shows 4. What is P(sum ≥ 9), in percent?
config.why: The space shrinks from 36 pairs to just 6 — only (4,5) and (4,6) qualify, so 2/6 = 1/3.
config.context: That is the entire meaning of the vertical bar: restrict, then recount.

activities.caption: the tree method, from first branch to self-check
activities.name: pbTreeOrder

config.prompt: Build the 4-red/6-blue tree — order the steps:
items: First layer: branch into the first event's outcomes — red 4/10, blue 6/10
Second layer uses probabilities conditional on the path — from 'red': red 3/9, blue 6/9; from 'blue': red 4/9, blue 5/9
Multiply along a path: P(two reds) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15
Sum across paths: P(same colour) = 2/15 + 1/3 = 7/15, so P(different colours) = 8/15
Self-check: the three answers sum to 1 — a built-in guard against slips
config.why: At every node the tree forces the question conditional probability exists to ask: has anything changed?

activities.caption: does the order matter? file each selection
activities.name: pbCountSort

config.prompt: Order matters or it doesn't — file each counting problem:

items.label: gold, silver and bronze from eight runners — 8 × 7 × 6 = 336
five books arranged on a shelf — 5! = 120

config.why: Permutations count orderings; combinations divide out the r! internal orderings that no longer matter.

activities.caption: price the long run before the casino does
activities.name: pbEvEst

config.prompt: A £1 British lottery ticket: roughly what is the expected return, in pence?
config.why: About a 1-in-14-million jackpot chance plus a roof of smaller prizes — near 50p per £1. Play forever and you lose half a pound per play, on average.
config.context: Roulette's single number pays 35-to-1 but carries a 2.7% house edge — invisible in an evening, certain over years.

activities.caption: ten heads behind you — bet on the honest statement
activities.name: pbStreakPredict

config.q: You have watched a fair-looking coin land heads ten times in a row. Which statement is now the right one?
choices: The next toss is more likely tails — the run must even out
The next toss is exactly 50/50, and 'this coin is rigged' has become more likely than it was
The next toss is exactly 50/50, and nothing about the coin's fairness has changed
The count of heads must snap back toward half the tosses soon
config.why: Coins have no memory — but ten heads is genuine evidence about the mechanism. Distinguishing 'is the coin fair?' from 'what comes next, given this coin?' is the whole trick, and the law of large numbers shrinks the ratio while the gap typically grows.

activities.caption: two readings of one number — drag the divider
activities.name: pbLensCompare

config.prompt: The same rules, two meanings for 'probability' — drag the divider:

before.label: frequentist
before.text: probability is long-run frequency in repeated trials — the number the law of large numbers locks in

after.label: Bayesian
after.text: probability is degree of belief, updated by evidence — Laplace formalised much of it in 1812 while calculating the mass of Saturn from noisy data

config.why: Same rules either way; different answers to 'what does a probability mean' — and every serious statistician uses both lenses.
